Debt: cheaper, must be repaid on schedule, lender has no upside. Equity: more expensive (dilutive), no repayment obligation, investor shares upside.

The wrong mix breaks businesses. Too much debt = fragile to revenue shocks. Too much equity = excessive dilution.

core_concepts.title: The Preferred Stack
core_concepts.body:
Preferred equity sits above common in liquidation. Investors get their money back (1x liquidation preference) before founders/employees see anything.

Understand the preference structure of your cap table. 1x non-participating is standard; 2x participating is brutal; 3x+ is rare and signals desperation.

core_concepts.title: Cost of Capital Rises With Risk
core_concepts.body:
The risk-free rate (Treasury) is the floor. Every additional layer of risk adds basis points: corporate bond > junior debt > preferred equity > common equity > venture equity.

Startup equity costs 25-35%+ as a hurdle rate. That's what investors implicitly demand for the risk.

take_action.step: Map your current cap table (or create one if you don't have it)

take_action: Model your ownership % after a typical seed or Series A round
Understand your vesting cliff and acceleration provisions

lessons.title: Value vs. Terms

core_concepts.title: Valuation Is a Story
core_concepts.body:
Valuation is the price tag on the story you're telling. It's a function of metrics, comparables, and narrative — in roughly equal proportion at early stage.

The valuation you raise at sets the bar for future rounds. Too low = excessive dilution. Too high = down-round risk, talent attraction issues.

core_concepts.title: Pre-Money vs Post-Money
core_concepts.body:
Pre-money: company value BEFORE new investment. Post-money: pre-money + new investment.

$$\text{Post-Money} = \text{Pre-Money} + \text{New Investment}$$

Dilution = New Investment / Post-Money. A $5M raise on $20M pre = 20% dilution. The same $5M on $15M pre = 25%.

core_concepts.title: Liquidation Preferences
core_concepts.body:
Preferred stock gets paid back before common. 1x non-participating = preferred gets either 1x money back OR converts to common (whichever is higher). 2x participating = preferred gets 2x + share of remainder.

In a strong outcome, preferences barely matter. In a soft outcome, they determine who gets paid.

core_concepts.title: Anti-Dilution Provisions
core_concepts.body:
If you raise a down round, previous investors' shares get adjusted to maintain (or partially maintain) their percentage. Two flavors:

- **Full ratchet**: investor gets the new lower price. Brutal.
- **Weighted average**: investor gets adjusted based on size of down round. Standard.

Full ratchet is rare and a red flag in any term sheet.

core_concepts.title: Terms > Valuation
core_concepts.body:
A $50M valuation with bad terms (participating preferred, full ratchet, board control) is worse than a $30M valuation with clean terms.

Founders fixate on the headline number. Sophisticated raises focus on terms. The headline impresses the press; the terms determine your outcomes.

take_action.step: For your next raise, list the top 5 terms you'd negotiate over valuation.

take_action: Have a securities lawyer review your last term sheet (or template).
Calculate your post-money dilution scenario for next 3 rounds.

lessons.title: Architecture of Agreement / Negotiation

core_concepts.title: BATNA
core_concepts.body:
Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement. What happens if this deal doesn't close.

Your BATNA is your real negotiating power. Strong BATNA = ability to walk away credibly. Weak BATNA = you'll accept worse terms because you have no alternative.

core_concepts.title: ZOPA — Zone of Possible Agreement
core_concepts.body:
The range between the seller's minimum and the buyer's maximum where a deal is possible. If ZOPA exists, deal is possible. If not, walk.

Most failed negotiations are situations where ZOPA didn't exist but parties pretended it did. Honesty about ZOPA upfront saves weeks.

core_concepts.title: Anchoring
core_concepts.body:
The first number put on the table shapes every subsequent number. Anchor first when you have strong information; let them anchor when you don't.

The anchor doesn't have to be reasonable to influence — research shows even absurd anchors pull subsequent offers toward them.

core_concepts.title: Interests vs Positions
core_concepts.body:
A position is what someone says they want ('I need $100K'). An interest is the underlying need ('I need to make rent and pay tuition').

Negotiate to interests, not positions. Interests are usually compatible; positions usually aren't. The trick is surfacing the interest underneath.

core_concepts.title: The 70% Rule
core_concepts.body:
If you can solve 70% of what each side actually needs at acceptable cost, you have a deal. Don't optimize for perfect — optimize for adequate and signable.

Deals die in the last 5%, often because one side insisted on the last point. The math says: take the 70%, leave the rest.

take_action.step: Identify your BATNA before your next important negotiation

take_action: Research the other party's likely BATNA
Practice anchoring by making the first offer in a low-stakes situation

lessons.title: Exit Strategy Architecture / M&A Math

core_concepts.title: EBITDA Multiples
core_concepts.body:
Most M&A pricing is a multiple of EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization). Different industries trade at different multiples — software 10-15x, manufacturing 5-8x, services 3-6x.

$$\text{Enterprise Value} = \text{EBITDA} \times \text{Multiple}$$

Know your industry multiple. Improve EBITDA + improve multiple = compound value creation.

core_concepts.title: Revenue Multiples (SaaS-specific)
core_concepts.body:
High-growth SaaS often valued on revenue, not EBITDA (which is often negative). Public SaaS multiples range from 5-25x revenue based on growth rate, retention, gross margin.

The rough rule: 100x revenue per percentage point of NRR above 100%. NRR of 130% justifies ~30x revenue.

core_concepts.title: Strategic vs Financial Buyers
core_concepts.body:
Strategic buyer: another operating company. Will pay premium because of synergies (revenue, cost, cross-sell).

Financial buyer (PE): cares about returns. Will pay multiples consistent with their fund return targets.

Strategic typically pays 1.5-2x what a financial buyer would. Build a buyer list that includes both types.

core_concepts.title: Earnouts and Holdbacks
core_concepts.body:
Part of the purchase price contingent on future performance. Designed to bridge buyer/seller valuation gaps and align incentives post-close.

Earnouts often disappoint. The integration after close changes the conditions that produced your pre-close performance. Negotiate clear, achievable, controllable metrics.

core_concepts.title: The Exit Story
core_concepts.body:
Buyers don't just buy your numbers. They buy your narrative — why this business now, why it's worth their multiple, what it does for them strategically.

The exit story is a 6-12 month construction project. Build it deliberately into board materials, customer wins, talent hires. The story is half the price.

take_action.step: Define your preferred exit path (acquisition, IPO, or lifestyle)

take_action: Research comparable exits in your industry and their multiples
Identify the top 5 potential acquirers for your business right now

lessons.title: Startup Operating System / Scaling Pains

core_concepts.title: Stage-Specific Operating Systems
core_concepts.body:
The operating practices that work at $1M ARR break at $10M, and break worse at $100M. Every stage has its own OS.

Founders who try to scale the same playbook hit a wall around 50 employees, 50 customers, or 50 transactions per day. The playbook has to change.

core_concepts.title: The 0-1, 1-10, 10-100 Frame
core_concepts.body:
Reid Hoffman's lens. 0-1: founders do everything, no process needed. 1-10: first hires, light process, founder still in every call. 10-100: real management, real processes, founder mostly out of operations.

Most founders stuck at 1-10 don't know how to make the jump to 10-100. The jump is about systems, not effort.

core_concepts.title: Hiring Ahead of Pain
core_concepts.body:
Most founders hire reactively — when they can no longer keep up. The result: chronic understaffing, exhausted teams, missed opportunities.

The right cadence: hire 3-6 months ahead of when you'll need the person, so they ramp before the crisis arrives. Costs more in the short run; saves you in the long run.

core_concepts.title: Delegate to the Future Org
core_concepts.body:
Hire and structure for the company you'll be in 12-18 months, not the company you are today. Otherwise you're constantly restructuring.

The delegation pattern: instead of hiring a manager for the existing 3 people, hire someone who can build the function for the future 15. The bar is different.

core_concepts.title: Founder Mode Doesn't Scale
core_concepts.body:
The founder's habit of being in everything works at 5 people, fails at 50. The hardest scaling skill is letting go — choosing what NOT to be in.

The founders who scale to large companies make this trade consciously. The ones who don't end up as bottlenecks in their own businesses.

take_action.step: Identify the 3 systems that break first as you scale (people, process, tech).

take_action: Build a 90-day operating cadence: weekly metrics, monthly review, quarterly planning.
Pick one founder-dependency point and create a 60-day handoff plan.

lessons.title: Dashboards (Deep-Dive)

core_concepts.title: The dashboard hierarchy
core_concepts.body: Board (5-7 metrics, monthly). Executive (10-15 metrics, weekly). Operational (one team-specific dashboard, daily). Each level summarizes the level below.

core_concepts.title: Lead vs. lag indicators
core_concepts.body: Lag = revenue, churn. Lead = pipeline coverage, NPS, time-to-first-value. Lead indicators belong on every dashboard; lag indicators belong on board dashboards.

core_concepts.title: The dashboard test
core_concepts.body: For every metric, ask: (1) What decision does this drive? (2) What's the threshold that triggers action? If neither answer is sharp, kill the metric.

core_concepts.title: Why dashboards fail
core_concepts.body: Most fail by accretion — every quarter someone adds a metric, none get removed. Set a hard cap (e.g., 15 metrics per dashboard) and audit quarterly.

take_action.step: Audit every dashboard. Score each metric: action-driving (1) or vanity (0).

take_action: Cut every vanity metric this week.
Add one lead indicator per team. Wire it to a weekly review.

lessons.title: Value Creation Journey / Capital Allocation

core_concepts.title: Capital Allocation as Highest-Leverage Decision
core_concepts.body:
Where you put each marginal dollar — reinvest, return, acquire — compounds for decades. Buffett's claim: capital allocation is the most important skill a CEO can develop.

Most businesses are well-run operationally and poorly-run from a capital allocation perspective. The deltas come from where the money goes, not how hard people work.

core_concepts.title: The Five Options
core_concepts.body:
Every dollar of cash flow has five possible homes:

1. Reinvest in the existing business
2. Acquire other businesses
3. Pay down debt
4. Return cash via dividends
5. Buy back stock

The right mix depends on relative returns. Cash spent on Option 1 should earn more than Option 5 — or you should be buying back stock.

core_concepts.title: IRR vs ROIC
core_concepts.body:
Internal Rate of Return is the annualized return on a single project. Return on Invested Capital is the return on the total invested base.

$$\text{IRR} = \text{discount rate where NPV} = 0$$

Projects: rank by IRR. Capital allocation across projects: optimize ROIC of the portfolio.

core_concepts.title: MOIC (Multiple on Invested Capital)
core_concepts.body:
Total cash returned ÷ total cash invested. The simple version of investment performance.

$$\text{MOIC} = \frac{\text{Total Distributions}}{\text{Total Invested}}$$

A $10M investment that returns $35M = 3.5x MOIC. MOIC ignores time; IRR captures it.

core_concepts.title: Hurdle Rates
core_concepts.body:
Every potential use of cash should clear a hurdle rate — your minimum acceptable return. If a project doesn't clear it, the cash should go to the next-best option.

Most businesses do projects that earn 5-8% returns when their cost of capital is 12%. Every such project destroys value. They just don't realize it.

take_action.step: Map your value creation timeline: 12, 24, 36 months — what milestones drive each valuation step?

take_action: Identify which 2 metrics most affect enterprise value in your category.
Set quarterly capital allocation rules aligned to those metrics.

lessons.title: Managing Uncertainty / Strategic Bets

core_concepts.title: Expected Value
core_concepts.body:
The probability-weighted return across all possible outcomes.

$$\text{EV} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} P_i \times \text{Outcome}_i$$

A 30% chance of $1M + 70% chance of -$100K = EV of $230K. Positive EV bets compound over time even when individual bets lose.

core_concepts.title: Probability of Ruin
core_concepts.body:
The chance the bet kills you if it loses. Different from expected value — a positive-EV bet with high ruin probability is still wrong.

Never bet what you can't afford to lose, even at favorable odds. One ruin event ends the game.

core_concepts.title: Optionality
core_concepts.body:
Strategic bets that preserve future choices are worth more than bets that lock you in. Maintain optionality whenever the cost is reasonable.

A $1M investment that gives you the right (not obligation) to do something later is often worth more than $1M deployed immediately.

core_concepts.title: Asymmetric Bets
core_concepts.body:
Bets where the upside is much larger than the downside. Limited downside, unbounded upside.

Venture capital is built on this — most investments go to zero, but the ones that don't return 100x. Look for asymmetric bets in operating decisions too.

core_concepts.title: Process Over Outcome
core_concepts.body:
In high-uncertainty domains, judge bets by the quality of the process, not the outcome.

A well-reasoned bet that loses is still a good bet. A poorly-reasoned bet that wins was still a bad bet. Outcome bias destroys learning.

take_action.step: List your 5 highest-impact strategic uncertainties. Rate each for likelihood and impact.

take_action: For the top 2, define what observable signal would shift your strategy.
Schedule a quarterly scenario-planning review.

lessons.title: Intelligent Risk Selection / Risk Map

core_concepts.title: Risk vs Uncertainty
core_concepts.body:
Knight's distinction. Risk: probabilities are known (or can be estimated from data). Uncertainty: probabilities are unknown.

Financial markets, machine reliability — risk. Most strategic decisions — uncertainty. Different tools required for each.

core_concepts.title: Risk-Adjusted Return
core_concepts.body:
Return per unit of risk. The Sharpe Ratio formalization:

$$\text{Sharpe} = \frac{R_p - R_f}{\sigma_p}$$

Where Rp = portfolio return, Rf = risk-free rate, σ = standard deviation. Higher Sharpe = more return per unit of volatility. Used for investment portfolios; generalizes to operating decisions.

core_concepts.title: Risk Mapping
core_concepts.body:
Plot known risks on a 2x2 matrix: probability (low/high) by impact (low/high).

- High prob × high impact: address immediately.
- High prob × low impact: monitor and accept.
- Low prob × high impact: have a plan ready (insurance, contingency).
- Low prob × low impact: ignore.

core_concepts.title: Tail Risks
core_concepts.body:
Low-probability, high-impact events. Black swans. The 1-in-100 year flood, the cyber breach, the regulatory shock.

Most organizations under-prepare for tail risks because they look unlikely. Don't insure against them at full cost, but have plans ready. The cost of being wrong is asymmetric.

core_concepts.title: Risk Capital
core_concepts.body:
The portion of capital you can lose without breaking the company. Bets sized to risk capital can be aggressive; bets sized to total capital must be conservative.

The operator's question: what's our risk capital, and what fraction of it are we deploying on this bet?

take_action.step: Build a risk register: 10 entries, scored by likelihood × impact.

take_action: For your top 3 risks, document mitigation strategy + owner.
Run a pre-mortem on your next major commitment this week.

lessons.title: Exit Strategy / Exit Story

core_concepts.title: Build a Saleable Asset
core_concepts.body:
Many great-operating businesses are unsellable. Owner-dependent, no transferable systems, no clean financials.

The goal of exit-readiness isn't to sell — it's to *be able* to sell. Optionality. The business is more valuable when it doesn't depend on you.

core_concepts.title: The Exit Narrative
core_concepts.body:
Buyers buy a story, not just a balance sheet. The story includes why this business now, why it's worth a premium, what the buyer can do with it.

The story takes 12-24 months to build deliberately. The mistake is starting it 3 months before the process opens.

core_concepts.title: Strategic vs Financial Exit
core_concepts.body:
Strategic buyer: another operating company. Pays for synergies. Higher multiples. Slower process.

Financial buyer (PE): cares about returns. Pays for stand-alone economics. Faster process; lower price.

core_concepts.title: The Process Premium
core_concepts.body:
A well-run process with 4-6 bidders typically clears 30-50% higher than a one-on-one negotiation.

Process premium comes from competition. Hire a banker who runs structured processes for businesses your size. Their fee (1-3%) usually returns 10-30x in higher clearing price.

core_concepts.title: Post-Exit Reality
core_concepts.body:
Most founders are unprepared for life after exit. Identity tied to the business, sudden liquidity, freedom that feels like vertigo.

Plan the next chapter before you close. The founders who do well post-exit have something they're moving toward, not away from.

take_action.step: Write your exit thesis: who buys you, why, at what multiple?

take_action: Identify the top 3 strategic acquirers in your category. Map their recent deals.
Set 5-year milestones tied to the multiple you want to achieve.

lessons.title: Complex Human Systems / Ethics Compass

core_concepts.title: The Ethical Override
core_concepts.body:
Some decisions are not optimization problems. They're constraints. Don't lie to customers. Don't shortcut safety. Don't exploit information asymmetry.

The ethical override sits above strategy. Violating it for short-term gain destroys long-term value, every time.

core_concepts.title: Stakeholder Map
core_concepts.body:
Every business decision affects multiple stakeholders: customers, employees, investors, suppliers, community.

Decisions optimized for one stakeholder often impose costs on others. Sustainable businesses balance the map; extractive businesses don't.

core_concepts.title: The Newspaper Test
core_concepts.body:
Before any consequential decision, ask: how would I feel if this decision was the front-page story in the local paper tomorrow?

If the answer is 'embarrassed,' you have your answer. The exercise surfaces the rationalizations you've been making.

core_concepts.title: Short-term vs Long-term Trade-offs
core_concepts.body:
Most ethical breakdowns trade short-term gains for long-term costs. Lying to a customer wins this deal; loses the next 10 referrals.

Discount long-term costs less than short-term gains. The math almost always favors the ethical path.

core_concepts.title: Building Ethical Infrastructure
core_concepts.body:
Individual willpower fails. Build systems that make the ethical choice the default — clear policies, independent audits, accessible whistleblower channels, leadership that visibly punishes violations.

Culture eats individual ethics for breakfast, in both directions.

take_action.step: Audit your team's psychological safety with an anonymous 3-question survey.

take_action: Identify one ethical edge-case decision you've delayed. Decide this week.
Define your 5 cultural values with observable behaviors per value.

lessons.title: Business Anatomy Masterclass / Personal OS

core_concepts.title: The CEO's Three Jobs
core_concepts.body:
Patrick Collison's framing. The CEO has three irreducible jobs:

1. Set the strategy
2. Build the team
3. Don't run out of money

Everything else can be delegated. These three cannot. The CEO who delegates these has stopped being CEO.

core_concepts.title: Calendar as Strategy
core_concepts.body:
Where you put your time is your real strategy, regardless of what your strategy doc says. Audit your last 4 weeks of calendar.

If the audit doesn't match your stated priorities, the calendar is the truth. Restructure or rewrite the strategy to match.

core_concepts.title: Energy Management Over Time Management
core_concepts.body:
Time is a constraint; energy is the variable. A high-energy 4 hours beats a low-energy 10 hours.

Protect the energy peaks. Schedule deep work for the hours when you're sharpest. Schedule meetings for the rest.

core_concepts.title: The Two-Question Filter
core_concepts.body:
For every commitment: (1) am I the only person who can do this? (2) is this the highest-leverage use of my time right now?

If the answer to either is no, delegate or decline. Most CEOs say yes to too much because saying no feels rude. Saying yes to the wrong things is worse.

core_concepts.title: Personal Operating System
core_concepts.body:
The set of rituals, defaults, and decisions you don't have to remake each day. Sleep, exercise, reading, deep work, family time.

The more decisions you automate at the personal level, the more attention you have for the high-stakes ones.

take_action.step: Map your personal operating system: sleep, exercise, deep work, recovery. Score each (1-5).

take_action: Identify the weakest input and design a 30-day habit installation.
Schedule weekly personal review: what worked, what didn't, what to adjust.

lessons.title: Capstone Encore: 90-Day Plan

core_concepts.title: The 90-Day Forcing Function
core_concepts.body:
Set 90-day plans, not annual ones. The cycle is short enough to be concrete, long enough to do real work.

At the end of every 90 days: audit, adjust, set the next 90. Compound over years.

core_concepts.title: Three Bets Per Quarter
core_concepts.body:
Each 90-day cycle has three big bets. Not 12. Not 5. Three.

The three are aligned with the year's strategy. They have measurable outcomes. They're owned by named people. Focus is what makes quarterly planning work.

core_concepts.title: Weekly Cadence
core_concepts.body:
The 90-day plan executes through weekly rhythms. Monday: set the week's priorities. Friday: review what shipped, what slipped, why.

The weekly cadence is the connective tissue. Plans without rhythm produce slogans without execution.

core_concepts.title: The Retrospective Discipline
core_concepts.body:
Every 90-day cycle ends with an honest retrospective. What worked, what didn't, what we'd do differently.

Most retros are theater. Make this one substantive — name specific decisions, specific people, specific lessons. Pattern recognition compounds.

core_concepts.title: The Long Game
core_concepts.body:
Career-changing companies are built by people who execute 40+ consecutive 90-day cycles with discipline. Most flame out after 5-10.

The difference isn't intensity. It's sustainable rhythm. The marathon, not the sprint.

take_action.step: Draft your 90-day capstone plan: 3 strategic priorities × 3 measurable outcomes each.

take_action: Identify 1 person in your org who can own each priority.
Set a weekly capstone review for the next 13 weeks.

lessons.title: Marketing Funnel Fundamentals

core_concepts.title: The Leaky Funnel Diagnostic
core_concepts.body:
Most marketing spend is wasted on funnels with broken stages. Top-of-funnel attracts traffic that drops off before conversion. The waste is invisible because the top-of-funnel metrics look fine.

The diagnostic: track conversion at every stage. The lowest-conversion stage is the leak. Fix it before adding more spend.

core_concepts.title: Channel Mix Audit
core_concepts.body:
Different acquisition channels have different funnel profiles. Paid social may produce 10x the volume at 1/10th the conversion. Referrals produce less volume but convert 5-10x higher.

Audit channel by full-funnel value, not top-of-funnel cost.

core_concepts.title: The 'Stop Spending' Move
core_concepts.body:
When a channel's full-funnel economics don't work, the right move is to stop spending — not to spend more efficiently. Optimization can't rescue an unworkable channel.

Most growth teams resist this move because it feels like losing. The math says it's winning.

core_concepts.title: Compounding Channels
core_concepts.body:
Content, SEO, referrals, brand — slow-build channels that compound over years. Once they take hold, they produce traffic at near-zero marginal cost.

The paradox: investing in compounding channels feels bad short-term (low immediate ROI) and great long-term.

core_concepts.title: Attribution Reality
core_concepts.body:
Most attribution models lie. Customers touch multiple channels. The 'last touch' that gets credit was likely shaped by 5 earlier touches.

Use attribution models to inform, not prescribe. The full-funnel data tells more truth than any single attribution view.

take_action.step: Map your current marketing funnel — every stage from awareness to purchase.

take_action: Identify the single weakest conversion point. Run an experiment to improve it this month.
Build a one-page funnel dashboard reviewed weekly.

lessons.title: Brand Positioning & Messaging

core_concepts.title: The positioning template
core_concepts.body: 'For [target] who [problem], we are [category] that [unique benefit], unlike [alternative], because [proof].' Every word is a choice with explicit non-customers.

core_concepts.title: The one-word brand
core_concepts.body: Volvo = safety. Disney = magic. Apple = simple. Strong brands compress to one word. Your job is to choose the word, then defend it for a decade.

core_concepts.title: Message hierarchy
core_concepts.body: Position (one sentence) → pillars (3-5) → proof points (3 per pillar) → channel adaptations (copy variants). Every piece of content traces upward to the position.

core_concepts.title: How positioning fails
core_concepts.body: (1) Trying to be all things — diluted word. (2) Drifting position quarter to quarter. (3) Copying competitors' words instead of owning your own.

take_action.step: Fill in the positioning template. Test it with five customers — they should be able to recite the unique benefit.
Pick your one word. Audit your last 10 pieces of content for whether they reinforce it.

take_action: Build the message hierarchy doc. Brief every marketer.

lessons.title: Pricing Strategy

core_concepts.title: Value-based, not cost-plus
core_concepts.body: Cost-plus pricing leaves money on the table. Value-based pricing anchors to the customer's willingness-to-pay, which is set by the alternative they would otherwise use.

core_concepts.title: Three pricing models
core_concepts.body: (1) Penetration: price low to gain share. (2) Skim: price high to harvest early adopters, then lower. (3) Value-tier: multiple SKUs at multiple prices to capture different willingness-to-pay segments.

core_concepts.title: The price-volume curve
core_concepts.body: Plot revenue against price across customer segments. The optimum is rarely at either extreme. Test at 3-5 price points.

core_concepts.title: Anchoring and decoy effects
core_concepts.body: A high-priced option (anchor) makes the middle option look reasonable. A decoy option (asymmetrically dominated) pushes selection to the target SKU. Apply intentionally; both are well-studied behavioral effects.

take_action.step: Survey 20 customers on willingness-to-pay using the Van Westendorp method.
Test a 10% price increase on new customers for 30 days. Measure win-rate.

take_action: Build a three-tier pricing page. The middle tier should be the target SKU.

lessons.title: Content & Demand Generation

core_concepts.title: The demand pyramid
core_concepts.body: Top: awareness content (problem-aware audience). Middle: educational content (solution-aware audience). Bottom: comparison and proof content (product-aware audience). Every channel must produce all three.

core_concepts.title: Pillar + cluster model
core_concepts.body: Pick 5-10 pillar topics aligned to positioning. Each pillar gets one 2,000-word piece + 10-20 cluster pieces that interlink. Search engines reward topical depth.

core_concepts.title: Distribution > production
core_concepts.body: Most teams over-produce and under-distribute. For every hour of writing, spend three hours distributing across channels and formats.

core_concepts.title: The content-to-pipeline link
core_concepts.body: Tag every content piece by funnel stage. Track which pieces drive captured leads, demos, and closed-won. Kill content that doesn't move pipeline within 90 days.

take_action.step: Define your 5-10 pillar topics. Map them to positioning pillars.
Build a distribution checklist: 5 channels per piece, minimum.

take_action: Audit last quarter's content. Cut anything that produced zero attributed pipeline.

lessons.title: Customer Retention & Loyalty

core_concepts.title: Cohort retention curves
core_concepts.body: Plot retention by signup month. A flat curve above 0% = real value. A declining curve to 0% = leak. The shape diagnoses the problem before metrics do.

core_concepts.title: Activation = day-one retention
core_concepts.body: Most churn happens in the first 7-30 days. Define your activation event (the moment a user gets value) and engineer the product to drive every new user to it within minutes.

core_concepts.title: Loyalty program economics
core_concepts.body: A loyalty program is profitable only when (a) it increases purchase frequency or basket size, AND (b) the increase exceeds the program cost. Most loyalty programs fail (b).

core_concepts.title: Churn-cause taxonomy
core_concepts.body: Five churn causes: (1) didn't activate, (2) lost the need, (3) switched to competitor, (4) couldn't justify price, (5) bad support. Each has a different fix.

take_action.step: Plot cohort retention for the last 6 months. Identify the largest drop point.
Define your activation event. Measure time-to-activation. Optimize it.

take_action: Interview 5 churned customers. Classify each to one of the five causes.

lessons.title: Operations Excellence

core_concepts.title: Heroes Don't Scale
core_concepts.body:
Every early-stage organization runs on heroes — individuals who carry processes in their heads, fix everything by sheer effort.

Heroes are essential at 10 employees and impossible at 100. The transition to repeatable systems is the hardest organizational pivot.

core_concepts.title: Process as Memory
core_concepts.body:
A process is institutional memory written down. It lets the organization remember what works even when the people who figured it out leave.

Without written processes, every departure is a knowledge loss. With them, the system survives turnover.

core_concepts.title: The 5x/Week Threshold
core_concepts.body:
Any task done 5+ times a week deserves a process. Below that threshold, ad hoc is fine. Above it, ad hoc becomes the constraint.

The 5x/week rule cuts through the false choice between 'over-process everything' and 'process is bureaucracy.'

core_concepts.title: Templates Beat Memos
core_concepts.body:
A process document that's a long memo will be ignored. A process document that's a one-page checklist gets used.

Format for use, not for completeness. Templates that fit on a single page beat 10-page SOPs every time.

core_concepts.title: Continuous Improvement
core_concepts.body:
Once a process exists, the goal isn't to freeze it — it's to improve it. Quarterly review: what's working, what's friction, what should change.

Frozen processes become bureaucracy. Living processes are operating leverage.

take_action.step: Identify your top 3 operational metrics. Are they actually leading indicators?

take_action: Build a daily operating rhythm: 1 metric, 1 review, 1 standup.
Document one process that lives in someone's head — get it on paper this week.

lessons.title: Supply Chain & Inventory Management

core_concepts.title: Four inventory types
core_concepts.body: (1) Cycle stock: covers normal demand. (2) Safety stock: protects against variability. (3) In-transit: in motion through the chain. (4) Strategic: long-lead-time critical items. Manage each separately.

core_concepts.title: Key operational metrics
core_concepts.body: Inventory turns (COGS / avg inventory): higher = better. Days of inventory (365 / turns): lower = better. Stockout rate, forecast accuracy (1 - |actual-forecast|/actual). Track weekly.

core_concepts.title: The Bullwhip Effect
core_concepts.body: Small demand fluctuations at the consumer end amplify upstream. Cures: shared forecasts, smaller batches, faster cycle times, fewer tiers.

core_concepts.title: Resilience levers
core_concepts.body: Multi-source (multiple vendors per critical input). Near-shore (move closer to demand). Buffer the bottleneck. Visibility two tiers up.

take_action.step: Classify every SKU into the four inventory types. Set distinct policies per type.
Compute inventory turns and days-of-inventory monthly. Plot the trend.

take_action: Identify your single biggest supply chain risk. Build one resilience lever this quarter.

lessons.title: Quality Management & Six Sigma

core_concepts.title: OpEx = standard work + improvement
core_concepts.body: Two pillars: every team has a documented standard, and a regular cadence to challenge it. Without the first, chaos. Without the second, decay.

core_concepts.title: Process before tools
core_concepts.body: A new tool on a broken process amplifies the breakage. Map and standardize first, then automate the parts that earn it.

core_concepts.title: Lead measures over lag measures
core_concepts.body: Revenue is a lag measure. OpEx tracks the daily/weekly inputs that predict it — call volume, on-time delivery, defect rate, response time.

core_concepts.title: Visible work creates ownership
core_concepts.body: If you can’t see the work, you can’t manage it. Boards, dashboards, daily huddles — the same information in front of the same people, every day.

core_concepts.title: Continuous improvement compounds
core_concepts.body: 1% better per week = 67% better per year. Discipline = the rhythm: weekly retros, monthly process reviews, quarterly resets.

take_action.text: Pick your most important repeatable process. Write a 1-page SOP. Hand it to someone who’s never run the process — can they execute it?

take_action.step: Define 3 lead measures for that process. Each = a daily/weekly input number you can track on a whiteboard.

take_action: Schedule a weekly 15-minute retro for the team running that process. What worked, what didn’t, what we’ll change.

take_action.text: Identify the metric you’d want a dashboard to surface every Monday. Build the query (or the spreadsheet) this week.

lessons.title: Project & Program Management

core_concepts.title: The triple constraint
core_concepts.body: Scope, time, cost. Any two can be fixed; the third must flex. Pretending all three are fixed produces death-march projects.

core_concepts.title: RACI per workstream
core_concepts.body: Responsible (does the work), Accountable (one neck — owns the outcome), Consulted (provides input), Informed (kept in the loop). Two A's = nobody is accountable.

core_concepts.title: Stage-gates over Gantt charts
core_concepts.body: Define 3-5 stage-gates with clear exit criteria. At each gate, decide: continue, pivot, or kill. Stage-gates beat detailed Gantt charts in changing environments.

core_concepts.title: Why programs fail
core_concepts.body: (1) No portfolio view across projects. (2) Resource conflicts unresolved. (3) Dependencies discovered late. (4) Status reporting hides red flags. Solve with weekly cross-project review.

take_action.step: Pick your most important project. Define the three constraints — which is flexing?
Build a RACI for every workstream. Verify each row has exactly one A.

take_action: Convert Gantt views to stage-gates with explicit exit criteria.

lessons.title: Vendor & Partnership Management

core_concepts.title: Vendor tiering
core_concepts.body: Tier 1: strategic (irreplaceable, deep relationship). Tier 2: preferred (multi-sourced, contracts in place). Tier 3: transactional (commodity, low switching cost). Manage each tier differently.

core_concepts.title: The four-question vendor scorecard
core_concepts.body: (1) Delivers on time? (2) Quality meets spec? (3) Pricing competitive vs. market? (4) Risk profile acceptable (financial, geographic, regulatory)? Score quarterly.

core_concepts.title: Partnership structures
core_concepts.body: Reseller, integration partner, co-marketing, JV, OEM. Pick the structure that matches the customer overlap and the depth of joint commitment.

core_concepts.title: Partnership failure modes
core_concepts.body: (1) Misaligned incentives. (2) No executive sponsor on either side. (3) No mutual scorecard. (4) Channel conflict with existing customers. Pre-empt all four in the contract.

take_action.step: Tier your top 20 vendors. For each Tier 1, name the strategic risk.
Build the four-question scorecard. Send to all Tier 1/2 vendors quarterly.

take_action: Pick one partnership opportunity. Draft a mutual scorecard before signing.

lessons.title: Data-Driven Decision Making

core_concepts.title: Data ≠ Decision
core_concepts.body:
Most organizations confuse data infrastructure with decision-making. They build dashboards, hire analysts, run experiments — and still make decisions by HiPPO (highest-paid person's opinion).

The gap is closing the loop: data → insight → decision → action → measurement. Most companies stop at insight.

core_concepts.title: Speed vs Quality Trade-off
core_concepts.body:
Slow careful analysis produces better decisions; the world has moved before you decide.

Fast lower-quality decisions execute against today's reality.

The right balance depends on reversibility. Two-way doors: bias to speed. One-way doors: invest in quality.

core_concepts.title: Leading vs Lagging Indicators
core_concepts.body:
Lagging: what happened (revenue, churn, NPS at quarter-end). Leading: what will happen (pipeline coverage, product engagement, support ticket volume).

Manage the business with leading indicators. The lagging ones tell you what you already saw coming.

core_concepts.title: Statistical Significance ≠ Practical Significance
core_concepts.body:
An A/B test can show a statistically significant 1% improvement at high confidence. If the absolute lift is small, the win isn't worth the operational complexity.

Don't optimize for significance. Optimize for impact. Most A/B test wins below 5% don't survive contact with production.

core_concepts.title: The 80/20 of Metrics
core_concepts.body:
Most businesses have 3-5 metrics that capture 80% of what's happening. Pick them. Track them ruthlessly. Ignore everything else for the weekly operating cadence.

Metric proliferation creates noise. Discipline picks the signals.

take_action.step: Categorize your last 10 decisions: Type 1 vs Type 2. How many got the right rigor?

take_action: Pick one current decision. Walk it through the Decision Quality Six.
Build a decision log: date, decision, reasoning, expected vs actual outcome.

lessons.title: KPIs & Performance Dashboards

core_concepts.title: KPI selection criteria
core_concepts.body: A real KPI is (1) tied to a strategic objective, (2) measurable with one definition, (3) reviewable on a defined cadence, (4) actionable when out of range. Anything failing one criterion is not a KPI.

core_concepts.title: North Star + supporting
core_concepts.body: One North Star metric (e.g., weekly active customers). 5-10 supporting metrics that explain the North Star. Don't have a Tree of KPIs without a clear North Star.

core_concepts.title: Leading vs. lagging
core_concepts.body: Lagging KPIs report outcomes (revenue). Leading KPIs predict them (pipeline, NPS). Boards need lagging; operators need leading.

core_concepts.title: Dashboard governance
core_concepts.body: Quarterly: review the KPI list. Add new strategic priorities, retire obsolete ones. Without governance dashboards accrete clutter.

take_action.step: Identify your North Star metric. Verify every executive can recite it.
Map 5-10 supporting KPIs that explain the North Star.

take_action: Set a quarterly KPI governance review. Add it to the operating calendar.

lessons.title: A/B Testing & Experimentation

core_concepts.title: The experiment design checklist
core_concepts.body: (1) Single hypothesis. (2) Pre-registered metric. (3) Power calculation determining sample size. (4) Random assignment. (5) Pre-specified stopping criteria. Skip any step = invalid test.

core_concepts.title: Statistical significance vs. practical significance
core_concepts.body: A 0.5% lift at p<0.05 may be statistically significant but practically irrelevant. Set a minimum detectable effect that matters to the business.

core_concepts.title: The peeking trap
core_concepts.body: Looking at results mid-test and stopping when you see significance inflates false-positive rates dramatically. Use sequential testing if you must peek.

core_concepts.title: What to test, what not to test
core_concepts.body: Test high-volume, recurring decisions (landing pages, pricing pages, onboarding flows). Don't test one-off strategic choices — use judgment.

take_action.step: Pick your three most-trafficked decision points (signup, pricing, checkout). Build an experiment backlog.

take_action: Adopt the design checklist as a requirement before any test goes live.
Set up an experiment scorecard tracking velocity, win rate, and impact.

lessons.title: Forecasting & Scenario Planning

core_concepts.title: Four forecasting methods
core_concepts.body: (1) Top-down: market size × share. (2) Bottom-up: rep × quota or customer × ARPU. (3) Time series: extrapolate history. (4) Driver-based: traffic × conversion × AOV. Triangulate at least two.

core_concepts.title: Forecast quality dimensions
core_concepts.body: Calibration (90% intervals contain truth 90% of the time). Resolution (specific, not vague). Bias (systematic over/under-shooting). Track all three over time.

core_concepts.title: Four-corner scenario frame
core_concepts.body: Identify two critical uncertainties (e.g., regulation × demand). Build four scenarios at the corners. Plan for each. Re-evaluate when reality moves toward a corner.

core_concepts.title: When forecasts mislead
core_concepts.body: Forecasts overweight recent history. Black-swan events are by definition unforecastable. Use scenarios for the tail.

take_action.step: Build your next-quarter forecast using two methods. Compare and reconcile.

take_action: Identify your two largest uncertainties. Sketch the four-corner scenario.
Set up a monthly forecast retrospective: actual vs. forecast, what we learned.

lessons.title: Risk Management & Mitigation

core_concepts.title: The risk register
core_concepts.body: List every material risk. Score each by likelihood × impact. Document the mitigation strategy and the owner. Review quarterly.

core_concepts.title: Four mitigation strategies
core_concepts.body: (1) Avoid (don't take the risk). (2) Transfer (insurance, contract). (3) Mitigate (reduce likelihood or impact). (4) Accept (small enough to absorb). Every risk gets one of the four.

core_concepts.title: Tail risk vs. operational risk
core_concepts.body: Operational risks are frequent and small (system outage). Tail risks are rare and catastrophic (key customer concentration, regulatory shutdown). Manage each differently.

core_concepts.title: Pre-mortem ritual
core_concepts.body: Before any major commitment, ask the team: 'Imagine it's a year from now and this failed. Why did it fail?' Surfaces hidden risks before they materialize.

take_action.step: Build a risk register with at least 10 entries. Score every entry.

take_action: Pick your top three risks. Document the mitigation and the owner.
Run a pre-mortem before the next major launch or commitment.

lessons.title: Innovation & New Product Development

core_concepts.title: Strategy as Architecture
core_concepts.body:
Strategy isn't a deck or a slogan. It's the architecture of choices a business has made and will keep making. Each choice constrains future choices and shapes future opportunities.

The businesses with coherent strategies have decision-making that aligns across hundreds of small calls. The ones without have decision-making that contradicts itself constantly.

core_concepts.title: Three Strategic Questions
core_concepts.body:
From Roger Martin: every strategy must answer three questions:

1. **Where will we play?** What market, customer, geography.
2. **How will we win?** What advantage will we have.
3. **What capabilities and systems must we have?** What we'll need to build.

core_concepts.title: Coherence Test
core_concepts.body:
Strategy fails when components don't reinforce each other. Premium pricing + low-cost manufacturing = incoherent. Brand-driven differentiation + commodity distribution = incoherent.

The coherence test: does each piece of the strategy support the others? If yes, the strategy compounds. If no, internal contradictions erode advantage.

core_concepts.title: Strategy ≠ Aspirations
core_concepts.body:
Aspirations are what you want. Strategy is the choices you'll make to get there.

'Be the leading provider of X' is an aspiration. 'Focus on enterprise customers with high switching costs through a partner-led go-to-market' is a strategy.

core_concepts.title: Strategy as Evolving Bet
core_concepts.body:
Strategies must survive contact with reality. The plan that survives is the plan that updates as conditions change.

lessons.title: Disruption & The Innovator's Dilemma

core_concepts.title: Sustaining vs. disruptive innovation
core_concepts.body: Sustaining innovation makes existing products better for existing customers (incumbents win). Disruptive innovation starts inferior but accessible (incumbents ignore until too late).

core_concepts.title: The incumbent trap
core_concepts.body: Incumbents are rationally optimized for their best customers. The disruptor starts with under-served or non-consumers. By the time the disruptor moves upmarket, the incumbent's cost structure can't compete.

core_concepts.title: Three disruption patterns
core_concepts.body: (1) Low-end disruption (cheaper, simpler). (2) New-market disruption (serves non-consumers). (3) Business-model disruption (different cost or revenue structure).

core_concepts.title: Incumbent defense
core_concepts.body: Set up a separate business unit with its own P&L, governance, and culture. Let it eat the parent business before someone else does.

take_action.step: Map your industry's adjacent low-end and non-consumption segments. Who serves them today?
Identify one disruptive threat to your business. Is there a sustaining-only response, or do you need a separate unit?

take_action: Read 'The Innovator's Dilemma' (Christensen). It pays for itself in one strategic decision.

lessons.title: AI & Emerging Technology Strategy

core_concepts.title: The S-curve and the chasm
core_concepts.body: Every technology follows an S-curve: slow start, rapid adoption, saturation. The strategic question is where on the curve your industry sits and what the chasm to mainstream adoption looks like.

core_concepts.title: AI use-case framework
core_concepts.body: Three layers: (1) Automate (replace repetitive work). (2) Augment (make experts faster). (3) Reinvent (build products that weren't possible before). Most teams under-invest in layer 3.

core_concepts.title: Build vs. buy vs. partner
core_concepts.body: For infrastructure (LLMs, cloud): buy. For workflow tools: buy or partner. For your unique differentiator: build. Don't build commodity; don't buy your edge.

core_concepts.title: Failure modes
core_concepts.body: (1) AI-washing existing features. (2) Building before measuring user need. (3) Ignoring data quality. (4) No human-in-the-loop for high-stakes decisions. Each has a known fix.

take_action.step: List your top 10 workflows. Tag each as automate / augment / reinvent candidate.

take_action: Pick one workflow to ship an AI feature on in 30 days. Measure adoption and impact.
Build a data-quality scorecard. AI is only as good as the data it learns from.

lessons.title: Sustainability & ESG Strategy

core_concepts.title: The three pillars
core_concepts.body: Environmental (carbon, waste, water). Social (labor, community, diversity). Governance (board structure, ethics, transparency). Each has measurable metrics.

core_concepts.title: Materiality matrix
core_concepts.body: Plot every ESG issue by (1) importance to stakeholders, (2) impact on business. Focus on the upper-right quadrant. Don't try to lead on everything.

core_concepts.title: Scope 1/2/3 emissions
core_concepts.body: Scope 1: direct (company vehicles, factories). Scope 2: purchased energy. Scope 3: supply chain, customer use, end-of-life. Most companies' largest footprint is Scope 3 — measure it.

core_concepts.title: ESG as competitive advantage
core_concepts.body: For some categories (consumer goods, infrastructure), ESG positioning drives premium pricing and customer preference. For others (commodity B2B), it's table stakes. Know which you are.

take_action.step: Build your materiality matrix. Pick the top 3 ESG priorities.

take_action: Measure Scope 1 and 2 emissions baseline. Plan for Scope 3.
Tie one ESG goal to an executive's annual review.

lessons.title: The Future-Ready Leader (Capstone)

core_concepts.title: The four founder modes
core_concepts.body: (1) Builder (early — product and customer obsessed). (2) Operator (scale — process and team obsessed). (3) Strategist (mature — capital and category obsessed). (4) Steward (legacy — culture and continuity obsessed). Know which mode the company needs from you now.

core_concepts.title: Leadership as time allocation
core_concepts.body: Your calendar is your strategy. If your time is in operations meetings, you are operating. If it is with customers and capital, you are leading. Audit your calendar monthly.

core_concepts.title: The personal operating system
core_concepts.body: Sleep, exercise, deep work, recovery — these are not soft. They are the inputs to every decision you make. Treat them as core OPEX.

core_concepts.title: The compounding career
core_concepts.body: Every venture, every relationship, every reputation event compounds. Be the kind of leader whose name in five years opens doors. The discipline today is the doors tomorrow.

take_action.step: Audit your last four weeks of calendar. Categorize every hour. Do the percentages match your strategy?
Pick one personal OS habit to install this month (sleep, exercise, deep work, weekly review).
